items.content:
18 of the 20 best open models today are Mixture-of-Experts. Dense is basically over.

And yet the know-how to train a good MoE still lives mostly in the heads of a handful of teams.

So we spent 800k GPU hours running the experiments ourselves and wrote everything down. Super happy to finally release "The Ultimate MoE Training Handbook", free and open, organized around the questions training teams hit:
- how many experts, how big, shared or not?
- why is half my step spent in all-to-all, and how do I hide it?
- why is my run 25x slower with no error in the logs?
- softmax, sigmoid or sqrt(softplus) router, and why keep it in fp32?
- aux loss or DeepSeek's loss-free bias?
- upcycle a dense checkpoint or train from scratch?
- can I serve with fewer experts per token than I trained with?

⚠️ Warning: it's long (~70k words, budget a few days, sorry) but with 55 interactive figures, code you can run and numbers from our own runs.

Read it here: https://t.co/6XihlUrj92

items.title: Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Small, scoring 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence I...
items.content:
Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Small, scoring 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index - their plan to release its weights would make it the highest-scoring open weights model developed outside China based on current rankings

Inkling 2 Small is launching as a proprietary model, available first-party through @thinkymachines' Tinker platform and Tinker Playground, with weights to be released at a later date. Its score is up 18 points from Inkling Small, with ~4x as many output tokens per task. It matches @GoogleDeepMind's Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) and surpasses @XiaomiMiMo's MiMo-V2.6-Pro on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0.1.

Key takeaways:

➤ Large gains over Inkling Small, especially on agentic tasks: AutomationBench-AA rises from 5% to 46% and FrontierCode 2.0 from 5% to 25%. HLE-Diamond also rises from 12% to 29%.

➤ Different coding strengths from Claude Sonnet 5.5 (medium): Inkling 2 Small scores 25% on FrontierCode 2.0 vs. 11% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (medium), but 13% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 vs. 30%.

➤ Creative agentic scores above Claude Haiku 5.5 and Grok 4.7 on AA-3D: Inkling 2 Small also scores above Gemini 3.8 Flash on both AA-3D and Code2Video-AA, but behind Claude Sonnet 5.5 on both.

➤ Research-level physics improves, but trails Gemini 3.8 Flash (high): Inkling 2 Small scores 56% on CritPt v2, up from 34% for Inkling Small, vs. 65% for Gemini 3.8 Flash (high).

➤ Fewer hallucinations from more selective answering: On AA-Omniscience v1.1, the hallucination rate falls from Inkling Small's 61% to 27%, while accuracy rises from 32% to 34% and the attempt rate falls from 77% to 53%.

➤ ~4x as many output tokens: Inkling 2 Small averages ~150K output tokens per Intelligence Index task vs. ~37K for Inkling Small, ~31K for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (medium), and ~99K for Gemini 3.8 Flash (high).

➤ Almost 6x the cost of Inkling Small, but cheaper than several other models with similar Intelligence Index scores: Inkling 2 Small costs $1.18 per Intelligence Index task vs. $0.20 for Inkling Small, $7.77 for Gemini 3.8 Flash (high), and $10.02 for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (medium).

Key model details:

➤ Type: Proprietary reasoning model at launch; Apache 2.0 weights release planned (date unconfirmed)

➤ Modalities: Text and image input, text output

➤ Size: 594B total parameters / 17B active parameters

➤ Pricing: $0.30/$1.00 per 1M input/output tokens ($0.03 per 1M cached input tokens)

➤ Availability at launch: Tinker and Tinker Playground

Congratulations to the team at @thinkymachines on the release!

items.title: The era of System One Vision Model is here! Introducing VFlash: parsing the visual world in parallel...
items.content:
The era of System One Vision Model is here! Introducing VFlash: parsing the visual world in parallel at unmatched speeds for Physical AI.

Most embodied prediction tasks like object localization, robot trajectory planning, and dense 3D motion are fixed-length float vectors. For example, a bounding box is always 6 tokens, a 10-waypoint robot arm trajectory is 54: we know these beforehand. Instead of decoding one token at a time, we can output the entire geometric shape in one go. 

VFlash enables up to 12x faster action decoding and a 5.1x overall robot inference speedup on edge GPUs like the Jetson Thor and DGX Spark. What’s surprising is that it ends up even more accurate than the VLM backbone, with up to 61% lower 3D trajectory error. The intuition is that VFlash avoids the cascading errors of autoregressive decoding, where every coordinate is written in ink and every later point loses the chance to backspace.

Everything that moves will be autonomous, and everything autonomous will need to think on its own chip. The next inference revolution is physical reasoning at the speed of reflex.

And as always, it’s open paper, open source! Link in thread:

items.title: Hy4 from Tencent scores 35 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and is the #2 model from...
items.content:
Hy4 from Tencent scores 35 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and is the #2 model from a China-based AI lab

Hy4 is the latest model from @TencentHunyuan and is the successor to Hy3 released earlier this year. It scores 35 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, equal with Grok 4.7 (xhigh) and 1 point behind Claude Haiku 5.5 (max). Hy4 is the #2 model from a China-based AI lab, behind only Kimi K3.1 Pro, which scores 46. Hy4 is priced at $0.834/$2.501 per 1M input/output tokens.

Key takeaways:

➤ Hy4 excels at agentic coding tasks. Hy4 scores 31% on FrontierCode 2.0, compared to 32% for Claude Fable 5.1 (max). It is the leading model from a China-based AI lab, with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max) scoring 28% and Kimi K3.1 Pro scoring 25%. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, it scores 37%, the fourth-highest score among models from China-based AI labs

➤ Hy4 outperforms its peers on knowledge and reasoning. Hy4 achieves accuracy of 50% on AA-Omniscience v1.1, 1 point ahead of Kimi K3.1 Pro, but has a high hallucination rate of 89% compared to Kimi K3.1 Pro’s 37%. On HLE-Diamond, it scores 33% compared to Kimi K3.1 Pro’s 37%

➤ Hy4 offers a competitive Capability vs. Cost trade-off compared to to peers. With a Cost per Intelligence Index Task of $0.78, Hy4 (35) is 10-times cheaper than Grok 4.7 (xhigh, 35) and 13-times cheaper than Qwen3.8 Max (0902) (34) but almost twice as expensive as Claude Haiku 5.5 (max, 36)

Other model details:

➤ Context window: 1 million tokens

➤ Pricing: $0.834/$2.501 per 1M input/output tokens. Cache reads $0.042 per 1M tokens

➤ Multimodality: Text and image input, with text output

items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Americans just voted to ban data centers in their towns, and Elon says "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now."

• 76% of voters in the NBC exit poll said they'd oppose a new data center in their own community
• Ballotpedia counted 38 local data center measures on ballots this year across 8 states, 20 of them in Ohio
• 15 Ohio municipalities passed bans or restrictions, even as Meta and AWS plan $1B and $2B data centers in the state
• Data Center Watch counted at least 45 projects disrupted by local opposition in the second half of 2026
• Texas Gov. Greg Abbott called for an AI "epicenter" in September, then paused new data center permits after Democrat Gina Hinojosa pledged a halt
• Hinojosa says data centers already permitted in Texas can finish, which Gavin Baker estimates covers 2027 and well into 2028
• Eurasia Group's Heather West says the friction "doesn't stop the buildout," since permitted projects will largely go ahead

@theojaffee: "The voters really hate data centers. This is, like, a 70/30 or an 80/20 issue almost everywhere."

what I see from the outside: labs are becoming schelling points for money, redistributing it to an ecosystem they created to accelerate their own development

it's a symbiosis. the best data and RL environment companies now know where models will fail before the labs do, and the labs just buy what they propose. that feeds back into every lab at once

a lot of the "AI accelerating AI R&D" happens outside the lab

items.title: Nanbeige has released Nanbeige4.3-33B, an open weights model matching Qwen3.8 27B (xhigh) at 20 on t...
items.content:
Nanbeige has released Nanbeige4.3-33B, an open weights model matching Qwen3.8 27B (xhigh) at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 with stronger terminal use but weaker knowledge

@Nanbeige is the foundation model research team at BOSS Zhipin, the Chinese recruitment platform operated by Kanzhun Limited. Its dense 33B reasoning model is open weights under Apache 2.0, with text input and output only, a 524K-token context window, and is small enough to run locally on a laptop.

Key results:

➤ Competitive results at ~30B total parameters. Nanbeige4.3-33B and Qwen3.8 27B (xhigh) both score 20, compared with 6 for Muse Glimmer (high, 30B).

➤ Terminal use and physics reasoning are relative strengths. Nanbeige scores 30% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 16% on CritPt v2's Hard Subset, vs. 6% and 4% respectively for Qwen3.8 27B.

➤ Different strengths to Qwen3.8 27B despite the same overall score. Nanbeige beats Qwen3.8 27B on AutomationBench-AA (53% vs. 48%), but trails on AA-Briefcase v1.1 (1162 vs. 1391 Elo), FrontierCode 2.0 (11% vs. 15%) and HLE-Diamond (7% vs. 15%).

➤ High abstention and low hallucination rates on Omniscience. Nanbeige scores -4 on AA-Omniscience v1.1 vs. -6 for Qwen3.8 27B, with a hallucination rate of 18% vs. 29%. It answers fewer questions correctly (12% vs. 17%) and declines 71% of questions.

➤ Similar intelligence with more output tokens per task. Nanbeige used 158K output tokens per Intelligence Index task vs. 110K for Qwen3.8 27B, about 44% more.

Additional model details:

➤ Type: Open weights reasoning (Apache 2.0 license)

➤ Size: 33B total parameters (dense)

➤ Modalities: Text input and output only

➤ Context window: 524K

items.content_html:
Nanbeige has released Nanbeige4.3-33B, an open weights model matching Qwen3.8 27B (xhigh) at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 with stronger terminal use but weaker knowledge

@Nanbeige is the foundation model research team at BOSS Zhipin, the Chinese recruitment platform operated by Kanzhun Limited. Its dense 33B reasoning model is open weights under Apache 2.0, with text input and output only, a 524K-token context window, and is small enough to run locally on a laptop.

Key results:

➤ Competitive results at ~30B total parameters. Nanbeige4.3-33B and Qwen3.8 27B (xhigh) both score 20, compared with 6 for Muse Glimmer (high, 30B).

➤ Terminal use and physics reasoning are relative strengths. Nanbeige scores 30% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 16% on CritPt v2's Hard Subset, vs. 6% and 4% respectively for Qwen3.8 27B.

➤ Different strengths to Qwen3.8 27B despite the same overall score. Nanbeige beats Qwen3.8 27B on AutomationBench-AA (53% vs. 48%), but trails on AA-Briefcase v1.1 (1162 vs. 1391 Elo), FrontierCode 2.0 (11% vs. 15%) and HLE-Diamond (7% vs. 15%).

➤ High abstention and low hallucination rates on Omniscience. Nanbeige scores -4 on AA-Omniscience v1.1 vs. -6 for Qwen3.8 27B, with a hallucination rate of 18% vs. 29%. It answers fewer questions correctly (12% vs. 17%) and declines 71% of questions.

➤ Similar intelligence with more output tokens per task. Nanbeige used 158K output tokens per Intelligence Index task vs. 110K for Qwen3.8 27B, about 44% more.

Additional model details:

➤ Type: Open weights reasoning (Apache 2.0 license)

➤ Size: 33B total parameters (dense)

➤ Modalities: Text input and output only

➤ Context window: 524K

➤ API availability: No confirmed public first- or third-party APIs

items.content:
🎉 Day-0 support for @Baidu_Inc’s ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base with vLLM!

280B total parameters, 14B active per token. Pre-trained on 33.5T tokens, with 128K training context and up to 1M tokens for fine-tuning and inference. Open Base weights for domain adaptation, instruction tuning and RL research.

Code highlights: 82.3% HumanEval+ and 40.1% LiveCodeBench pass@1 (both 1-shot), versus 69.5% and 31.9% for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base under the same evaluation setup.

Efficiency is built into the architecture: 37 compressed-attention layers + 6 MLA-DSA layers, Multi-Router Latent MoE, and ECHO — reusing the final layer as a speculative draft.

Serve FP8 or BF16 with Baidu’s vLLM-ERNIE plugin on vLLM 0.32.0. ECHO runs through vLLM’s MTP path; recipes include expert parallelism, KV offload and prefill/decode disaggregation, with runs verified on @NVIDIA GB200 and H100.

Weights are on @huggingface and @ModelScope2022.

Recipe: https://t.co/OhlAm9XYKB
FP8: https://t.co/pzNsf3LBb9
BF16: https://t.co/igWS26BQ62

items.summary: Thom Wolf (NVIDIA) gives a technical answer on MoE design: at fixed total and active parameters, finer-grained experts help up to a point — one ablation showed loss dropping until 128 experts (each 1/4 width, top-8), with most released models using 128-384 experts and top-4 to top-8 routing; beyond that, smaller GEMMs and all-to-all communication overhead eat into step time, so the practical expert count is somewhat less sparse than loss alone suggests. items.content_html:
@wleatherman9 @Nouamanetazi @lvwerra @huggingface short answer from the handbook: at fixed total and active params, finer experts help up to a point. in one ablation the loss kept dropping until 128 experts (each 1/4 width, top-8), then nothing more (most released models sit at 128 to 384 experts, top-4 to top-8)

past that, smaller GEMMs and more all-to-all traffic start eating your step time, so the best count on your cluster is usually a bit less sparse than the loss alone says.

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber exploited 948 Linux bugs and came up with hacking techniqu...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber exploited 948 Linux bugs and came up with hacking techniques that Linux experts say they hadn't seen before.

• It found 81 previously unknown high-severity Firefox vulnerabilities, and Mozilla has started shipping fixes
• 588 of the 948 Linux kernel bugs it exploited had never been found before
• Out of 166 exploits sampled, 10 used techniques that kernel experts said looked new, some letting a local attacker gain root
• It went beyond its intended scope in 0.07% of honeypot tests, vs 5.51% for GPT-5.6 Cyber
• OpenAI rates it "Critical" for cybersecurity, the highest risk level in its Preparedness Framework
• Only approved Daybreak Red customers can use it for now, through the API and Codex
• Noma Security's Chris Hughes points to OpenAI's own dashboard showing under 25% of found bugs fixed, and warns that discovery without fixes raises risk

@theojaffee: "My sense is that a model that you specifically task with being really good at offensive cyber is kind of more likely to be misaligned by its nature... it's kind of like gain of function research."

items.title: Wayve's Brandon Basso demos how its self-driving AI learns what safe driving looks like, rather than...
items.content:
Wayve's Brandon Basso demos how its self-driving AI learns what safe driving looks like, rather than relying on HD maps and external safety checkers:

"The way that we've built the driving stack is with safety as an intrinsic property vs an extrinsic bolt-on property."

"Lots of systems have high-definition maps that are really like checkers. What if the stop sign isn't there? What if it moved? What if there's a temporary stop sign? What if the stop sign is connected to a bus that's moving?"

"The checker systems tend to be the ultimate bottleneck and limit of system performance."

"What you see on the screen here is a learned representation of safety. You can think of this as like a future occupancy map. The red areas are the don’t drive in areas."

"We use this system not as a bolt-on checker, but as an explicit head, a task that we learn, on how to drive safely."
@wayve_ai

• Its RoboFab factory in Salem, Oregon is designed to build up to 10,000 robots a year

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: OpenAI just promised to cover its data centers' power costs and stop making pub...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: OpenAI just promised to cover its data centers' power costs and stop making public officials sign NDAs.

• OpenAI released its National Community Compact and Compute Campus Policy Blueprint 2 days after the midterms
• Incoming governors Gina Hinojosa in Texas and Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia have called for pausing data center development
• OpenAI will pay for the power its future company-owned campuses use and the infrastructure to supply it, and shield other ratepayers if a project gets delayed or canceled
• It will stop using most NDAs with public officials, with exceptions for security information and trade secrets
• It will also fund local services like childcare, education, healthcare and transportation
• The blueprint asks utility regulators to hold other large power users to the same rules
• Chris Lehane says the blueprint has been in the works since August and predicts AI will be the "number-one issue of the 2028 presidential election"

@theojaffee: "It's a failure of governance that, like, why does OpenAI have to, like, pay for local community priorities? Like, shouldn't the local community have an entity that raises revenue to pay for priorities on their behalf called their local government?"

items.title:
Fixed the mobile stretched interface on portrait mode in BF1942  by modding the engine

Claude Code ...
items.content:
Fixed the mobile stretched interface on portrait mode in BF1942  by modding the engine

Claude Code told me how it did it:

"1. Spotting the HUD: 3D world draws use a perspective projection, where far things look smaller. The HUD uses a flat one. I can tell them apart from the projection matrix the game sets before each draw.

2. Measuring each element: before drawing a HUD piece (the ticket count, the map, an ammo icon), I calculate on the CPU where its corners land on screen. That uses the same matrix math the graphics card would do.

3. Squeezing it back: I shrink its height by that 2.9× factor toward a fixed edge depending on where it sits. Things at the top move toward the top edge, things at the bottom toward the bottom edge, and things in the middle toward the center. Because everything in the same band moves together, the map and its icons stay lined up.

4. Leaving some things alone: big panels, like the scoreboard and loading photo, keep the old stretch so their layout isn't changed. On menu and loading screens, text shrinks around its own center so tap areas don't move."

items.title: FLUX 3 Image Klein is the #2 open weights model on AA-Image-T2I v2.1, neck and neck with #1 Qwen-Ima...
items.content:
FLUX 3 Image Klein is the #2 open weights model on AA-Image-T2I v2.1, neck and neck with #1 Qwen-Image-2.1, and #3 among open weights models on AA-Image-Editing v2.1

FLUX 3 Image Klein is Black Forest Labs' 5.6B parameter open weights image model, released on October 15 under the FLUX Kommunity License. The license is free for non-commercial use, and commercial use of outputs is allowed for individuals and companies with under $5M USD in annual revenue. It joins FLUX 3 Image, released on October 1, which ranks #13 on AA-Image-T2I v2.1 and #15 on AA-Image-Editing v2.1. Both models support Text to Image and Image Editing, and we evaluated both at 1K resolution through BFL's API, which applies BFL's prompt upsampler.

FLUX 3 Image Klein is priced at $0.009 per image ($9 per 1k images) at 1K resolution on the BFL API, 40% below FLUX.2 [klein] 9B on BFL's API. FLUX 3 Image is priced at $0.048 per image ($48 per 1k images). Klein is available through the BFL API and the BFL Playground, with open weights on Hugging Face. FLUX 3 Image is available through the BFL API, fal and OpenRouter.

Congratulations to @bfl_ai on the FLUX 3 Image family!

See below for our analysis and example outputs of FLUX 3 Image Klein and FLUX 3 Image in the Artificial Analysis Image Arena 🧵

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Zipline just raised $1.5B at a $21.5B valuation, and Walmart is adding 300 more...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Zipline just raised $1.5B at a $21.5B valuation, and Walmart is adding 300 more drone delivery sites.

• The valuation is nearly 3x where it was in January, when Zipline raised over $600M at about $7.6B
• Zipline and Walmart run 21 drone sites today in Texas and Arkansas, so the new deal grows that network about 15x
• The median October order arrived 19 minutes after checkout, versus 30+ minutes for ground delivery
• Zipline made over 1M deliveries in Dallas-Fort Worth this year
• Its factory near SFO can build up to 20,000 aircraft a year
• Uber partnered with Zipline in August and is targeting 1M drone deliveries a day by 2029
• Walmart also works with Alphabet's Wing, and Amazon is expanding its drone service to about 500 US locations

@sophiadew: "I actually had the opportunity of visiting the Zipline factory down in South San Francisco earlier this month and got to see all these drones in person."

items.title: Nooks CEO @_dan_lee_ predicts AI's next major breakthrough won't just be better reasoning, but under...
items.content:
Nooks CEO @_dan_lee_ predicts AI's next major breakthrough won't just be better reasoning, but understanding how to persuade humans, with sales data potentially holding the key:

"In coding, when a coding agent is generating code, it'll pull in relevant parts of the code base."

"In sales, when you're trying to prepare for a meeting or send an email to someone, you actually wanna pull in relevant sales scenarios, but then there's this question, what's a relevant sales scenario?"

"Nooks sits at this unique position where we own the layer between the sales rep and their end customer."

"There's just been less data on persuasion in the training sets for frontier models because persuasion is all about understanding what people think, and that’s not observable."

"Sales, I think, is the richest data set on persuasion because it's the most concrete business application. Models are gonna become a lot better, not just at reasoning, but at persuasion, which is gonna change sales."
@NooksHQ

items.title: Inkling 2 Small makes large gains over Inkling (xhigh) on AA-3D and Code2Video-AA, with scores close...
items.content:
Inkling 2 Small makes large gains over Inkling (xhigh) on AA-3D and Code2Video-AA, with scores close to Muse Spark 1.3 and Qwen3.8 Max, respectively.

AA-3D tests models’ ability to create interactive 3D experiences. Inkling 2 Small scores 1021 Elo vs. 966 Elo for @GoogleDeepMind's Gemini 3.8 Flash and 1033 Elo for @AIatMeta's Muse Spark 1.3 (max).

On Code2Video-AA, which tests models’ ability to create videos using code, Inkling 2 Small scores 1020 Elo vs. 899 Elo for Gemini 3.8 Flash and 1021 Elo for @Alibaba_Qwen's Qwen3.8 Max (0902) (xhigh).

Compared with Inkling (xhigh), it gains 438 Elo on AA-3D (1021 vs. 583) and 553 Elo on Code2Video-AA (1020 vs. 467).

"The pace of the frontier, both from the labs as well as our own applied research, makes us really confident that sales is gonna be the next job to inflect."

Meet Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash ⚡️

We’ve made the model more cost-effective, bumped the video generation...
items.content:
Meet Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash ⚡️

We’ve made the model more cost-effective, bumped the video generation and editing limit up to 15 seconds, and made updates to how scenes hold together over time. We've also given character speech an upgrade, reduced visual glitches like jump cuts, and made sure the model stays even truer to any reference assets you upload.

So… what does all of that actually mean for you?

It gives you more room to tell your story. With up to 15 seconds to work with, you have more flexibility to create what you need — videos look more cinematic and smooth, offering stronger consistency that keeps objects anchored from start to finish. And when characters speak, the dialogue sounds more fluid and natural.

Creators and everyday users can start directing scenes and multi-turn edits in @FlowbyGoogle, generating 15-second clips at no additional cost in Google Vids, or creating 15-second videos in the @GeminiApp. Plus, for developers and businesses building with the API, we've dropped the price by 30% from the previous generation, making it available at just $0.07 per second for 720p video.

Watch the model in action as it turns a single style frame into a 4-shot, 15-second macro science explainer of a living beehive ↓

items.title: @_quanta_ @TheVixhal @divagr1925 yeah kind of but not an external inference engine, detection and ex...
items.content:
@_quanta_ @TheVixhal @divagr1925 yeah kind of but not an external inference engine, detection and execution happen inside the forward pass via compiled circuits

qwen emits the tool-call tokens, those circuits key on the fixed tokens in qwen’s tool-call format (=name, =text, >, </tool_call>, etc.). when the call closes, the circuit runs the operation in its own state (DeltaNet tables for qwenFS, or the compiled CPU in qwenputer) and then forces the subsequent tokens of the <tool_response> itself. qwen’s layers never see a raw tool call that still needs executing

items.title: FLUX 3 Image Klein and FLUX 3 Image rank above their FLUX.2 predecessors in all 19 Text to Image cat...
items.content:
FLUX 3 Image Klein and FLUX 3 Image rank above their FLUX.2 predecessors in all 19 Text to Image categories

Our Image Arena taxonomy measures 9 capabilities and 10 use cases for Text to Image. Capabilities measure what a prompt asks the model to do. Use cases measure how those capabilities combine in the workloads end users run.

Both models improve on their predecessors in every Text to Image category. Layout is a top gain for both, alongside Knowledge for Klein and Complex Compositions for FLUX 3 Image. Klein climbs from the bottom third of the board into the top quarter on Knowledge and Layout, and FLUX 3 Image is now in the top ten for Complex Compositions, Reasoning and Knowledge.

➤ Knowledge: prompts that need real-world knowledge to get right, such as a named landmark, a specific animal or plant species, or a scientific process

➤ Layout: structured composition, such as flowcharts with arrows, block diagrams, multi-panel pages and a clear visual hierarchy between elements

➤ Complex Compositions: precise counting, spatial relationships, subject interactions and attribute binding

Among editing actions, FLUX 3 Image Klein and FLUX 3 Image both improve most in Composition & Framing over their FLUX.2 predecessors

Our Image Arena taxonomy measures 7 editing actions and 10 use cases for Image Editing. Editing actions measure what an edit asks the model to do.

Composition & Framing is the biggest editing-action gain for both models: FLUX 3 Image jumps from the bottom third of the board into the top ten, and Klein into the top quarter. Reasoning-Based Edit is the next-biggest gain for both. Identity Preserving Edit remains a relative weak spot for both models.

➤ Composition & Framing: cropping, extending, reframing, and changes to camera view or perspective

➤ Reasoning-Based Edit: edits that need inference about the scene rather than a literal instruction

➤ Identity Preserving Edit: changes to people, faces and characters that must keep their identity intact

items.title: The best way to manage the complexity of a large application portfolio is *consistency* across every...
items.content:
The best way to manage the complexity of a large application portfolio is *consistency* across every app.

OutSystems is a platform for building and deploying enterprise-grade software. Its main benefit is a consistent way to deliver software.

Here is a link to the OutSystems MCP server: https://t.co/fuLPR397cq

There are two fundamental ideas here:

1. Every screen, dataset, and business logic across all of your applications lives in a shared application model.

2. The platform compiles that application model and provides the runtime, deployment lifecycle, security controls, and monitoring.

As the team builds more applications, they can rely on the consistency of their shared application model.

This significantly reduces the complexity.

You can use OutSystems MCP to give Codex, Claude Code, or any other coding agent access to the shared application model and the platform tools.

For example, your coding agent can inspect the application's existing screens, data, and business logic in OutSystems before deciding how to maintain the codebase.

It can also ask OutSystems to move the application through the deployment process.

Your coding agent inspects the existing structure, coordinates the change, and helps you publish and deploy it.

Here is more information on how to use OutSystems to manage the chaos agents create: https://t.co/9RVg9JR9lK

Thanks to the @OutSystems team for partnering with me on this post.

items.content:
Git Magic by Ben Lynn is now in @ChapterPal's collection of open books.

Git is a free, open-source distributed version control system (VCS) designed to track changes in source code and manage project history over time.

Created by Linus Torvalds in 2005, it is the industry standard for software development, allowing multiple developers to work on the same codebase simultaneously without overwriting each other's work.

(It's incredible that Linus didn't name Git after himself!)

ChapterPal has two versions of the book to choose from: the author's original version (2010) and an updated version from ChapterPal (2026).

Git is a free, open-source distributed version control system (VCS) designed to track changes in source code and manage project history over time.

Created by Linus Torvalds in 2005, it is the industry standard for software development, allowing multiple developers to work on the same codebase simultaneously without overwriting each other's work.

(It's incredible that Linus didn't name Git after himself!)

items.title: Crazy stuff. I have a Substack newsletter. A user can subscribe for free or choose to support me as ...
items.content:
Crazy stuff. I have a Substack newsletter. A user can subscribe for free or choose to support me as an author and subscribe for a monthly fee.

The user can also choose to "save" and subscribe for a yearly fee, which Substack will renew the following year.

A user subscribed last year for this renewable yearly fee. A week ago, their card was charged by Substack for one more year of the subscription.

The user seemingly didn't like that, so instead of contacting Substack and explaining the situation, they requested a refund from their bank, accusing me of "not providing the product" they paid for.

I would love to refund the user; I don't force anyone to support me. Sometimes we forget to cancel a recurring charge. This happens.

However, check the math. This is crazy:

1. Substack already charged me (not the user) an $11 platform commission.
2. Stripe already charged me (not the user) a $4.37 payment processing fee.
3. Stripe already charged me (not the user) a $15.00 "dispute fee."

So, I was already charged a nonrecoverable $30.37. If I refund the user $110, which I would gladly do, the user will walk away happy, Substack and Stripe will walk away happy, and only I will walk away with a $30.37 loss.

If I decide not to do anything, Substack and Stripe will dispute the charge on my behalf, and I might "win."

If Stripe Smart Disputes wins, using its 30% "success fee," I will keep $46.63.

If Substack counters through the manual process and wins, I don't know how much I will keep, but most likely less than $46.63.

This is just crazy. I don't have another word. Either the user gets ripped off or I do. I didn't do anything wrong. The user just forgot to cancel the renewal.

items.content:
@realdarin Actually I did a lot of consumer research going around USA before AI was a thing. There was a LOT of anti tech feeling back then. 

What you laid out has just increased that anger.

There's a reason why kids leave these neighborhoods and go somewhere else to build a career. 

They are very conservative (read they don't want anything to change). 

Hard to change them. And you hear how rude and anti American they are.

The America I used to live in used to give people a chance to talk, present what they are gonna present, and then line up to have their concerns heard.

This America is just shouting.
